query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high‐entropy alloys, modest levels of Al promote local chemical ordering within the predominantly entropy‐stabilized single-phase fcc matrix, forming nanoscale coherent precipitates at internal boundaries. These nanoscale ordered domains act both as obstacles to dislocation motion and as effective sinks for radiation‐induced defects, thereby enhancing high‐temperature strength, environmental and radiation resistance while preserving low stacking fault energy necessary for deformation twinning at cryogenic temperatures. In contrast, excessive Al drives overt ordering that yields coarse second phases and undermines cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, equiatomic fcc Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with low Al content showing minimal inhomogeneity.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al concentration (or tailor post-casting heat treatments) while keeping the other elemental ratios constant.
generation.conditions: Testing performed under controlled thermomechanical conditions including high-temperature loading, radiation exposure, and cryogenic mechanical testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale chemical ordering/precipitates that form at internal grain or phase boundaries within the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: The configurational entropy of the multi-component alloy favors a single fcc phase at moderate temperatures, yet Al’s strong tendency for chemical ordering induces localized nanoscale domains. These small ordered regions strengthen the material by serving as obstacles to dislocation motion and by trapping radiation-induced defects without increasing the stacking fault energy excessively, thus allowing the retention of deformation twinning-driven cryogenic toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Within an optimal Al-content window (e.g., moderate Al additions), the alloy will exhibit increased high-temperature strength and radiation resistance (via impeded defect migration) and maintain or improve cryogenic toughness due to the preservation of low stacking fault energy and activation of twinning. Exceeding this window will lead to coarse precipitate formation, reducing the desirable toughness and ductility.
generation.baseline: An Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy with minimal Al addition demonstrating a homogeneous fcc solid solution and baseline mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only within a compositional range where Al remains below the threshold for macroscopic phase separation and under processing conditions that prevent full-scale ordering; outside this window, the balance between entropy stabilization and ordering is lost.
generation.uncertainty: The precise Al concentration threshold and the effect of processing variables (e.g., cooling rate, aging conditions) on the precipitate size, distribution, and their influence on stacking fault energy require further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEA samples with systematically varied Al content (for example, low, moderate, and high levels) while keeping the other elemental concentrations fixed. Subject each sample to identical thermomechanical processing. Then, characterize the microstructure using high-resolution TEM and atom probe tomography to assess the presence, size, and distribution of nanoscale chemically ordered regions. Perform mechanical testing at high temperatures, under controlled radiation exposure, and at cryogenic temperatures to measure strength, defect accumulation, and fracture toughness.
measurements: TEM/atom probe tomography for nanoscale ordering and precipitate characterization
Tensile and hardness tests at high temperature
Irradiation tests followed by defect density analysis
Tensile and fracture toughness tests at cryogenic temperatures
Stacking fault energy evaluation via indirect measurement or simulation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If altering the Al concentration does not lead to a correlated change in the formation or characteristics of nanoscale ordered domains and the corresponding mechanical and radiation resistance properties do not improve relative to the baseline in the moderate-Al samples (or if overly high-Al samples do not show a degradation), then the hypothesis that the interplay between configurational entropy and Al-induced local ordering governs the phase stability and property retention is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Compared to high-entropy alloys, medium-entropy alloys exhibit lower mixing entropy, typically ranging from R to 1.5R (where R is the gas constant). MEAs generally comprise three to four principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions, representing an intermediate class of multi-component alloys that bridge the gap between conventional alloys and HEAs [,]. Unlike HEAs, MEAs possess relatively lower compositional complexity, which allows for better control over microstructure and phase stability while still retaining desirable mechanical and thermal properties. Among these, CoCrNi-based MEAs have attracted considerable attention in recent years, driven by their promising performance and the rapid increase in related research efforts [,,]. They exhibit not only excellent mechanical strength and ductility at elevated temperatures but also outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures [].

Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study AlxCrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. High-entropy alloys have good application prospects in nuclear power plants due to their excellent mechanical properties and radiation resistance. In this paper, the microstructure of the Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 high-entropy alloy was researched using metallurgical microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and scanning electron microscopy. The mechanical properties were tested using a Vickers microhardness tester and a tensile testing machine, respectively. The results showed that Co32Cr28Ni32.94Al4.06Ti3 had a single-phase, disordered, face-centered, cubic solid-solution structure and was strengthened by solid solution. The alloy lattice parameter and density were estimated as 0.304 nm and 7.89 g/cm3, respectively. The test results indicated that the alloy had satisfactory mechanical properties with yield stress and tensile strength of about 530 MPa and 985 MPa, respectively.
